articles.title: The active self in autism: multisensory and sensorimotor foundations of bodily self-representation
articles.authors: Amir Jahanian Najafabadi, Alireza Rastegari
articles.abstract: The active self, understood as the embodied sense of self arising from goal-directed action and interaction with the environment, is supported by sensorimotor processes including multisensory integration and proprioception. Atypical self-representation in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has been proposed to relate to differences in these processes. To clarify this relationship, we conducted a systematic conceptual review of 37 empirical studies published between 2010 and August 2025 examining multisensory and bodily components of the active self in ASD. The literature was synthesized across three themes: (1) multisensory integration, (2) self-bias and self-other differentiation, and (3) motor underpinnings of bodily awareness. Across studies, autistic participants frequently showed differences in multisensory timing and weighting, including reduced or delayed susceptibility to some bodily ownership illusions and greater reliance on proprioceptive or immediate sensory information. Evidence also indicated differences in the flexibility of peri- and interpersonal space, self-other differentiation, agency-related processing, and motor planning and execution. However, findings were not uniform across paradigms, developmental stages, or participant groups, with relatively preserved performance reported under some unimodal or low-noise conditions. Together, these findings support an association between multisensory and sensorimotor processing and several components of bodily self-representation in autism, while substantial methodological and sample heterogeneity limits strong causal or clinical conclusions. Future research should prioritize larger and more representative samples, longitudinal and multimethod designs, standardized experimental paradigms, and objective measures of embodiment to determine whether these mechanisms can ultimately inform individualized assessment and intervention.Clinical trial number Not applicable.

articles.title: Artificial general intelligence and public diplomacy: A scenario analysis of possible futures
articles.authors: Mahdi Mahdavi Athar
articles.abstract: Does the potential advent of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) render traditional public diplomacy obsolete? While scholars have extensively documented the integration of narrow AI into diplomatic practice, we still lack a structural understanding of how AGI might redefine the very mechanics of international persuasion. Public diplomacy serves as a critical testing ground here, sitting at the volatile intersection of legitimacy, persuasion, and algorithmic mediation. In this study, I offer three primary interventions. First, I conceptualize Computational Narrative Power (CNP) as an actor's capacity to optimize persuasive narratives at scale, relying on production volume, targeting precision, adaptive responsiveness, and attributional opacity. Second, I map four plausible AGI futures based on the interplay between technological diffusion and global governance architectures: Soft Hegemony, Collective Smart Diplomacy, Narrative Cold War, and Digital Anarchy. Rather than predictive prophecies, I treat these scenarios as analytical stress tests demonstrating that governance structures dictate international stability just as much as technological breakthroughs. Finally, I identify an inherent transparency-efficiency trade-off in automated statecraft, arguing that AGI compels us to shift our analytical gaze from mere message dissemination to the governance of underlying epistemic infrastructures. • Introduces Computational Narrative Power (CNP) in AGI-driven public diplomacy. • Explores four AGI futures using Schwartz's 2x2 scenario planning matrix. • Analyzes AGI capability distribution and international governance models. • Highlights the critical role of anticipatory governance for systemic stability.

articles.title: Temporal signatures of prediction error reveal external forces on an embodied robot
articles.authors: Pierre Klintefors, Birger Johansson, Christian Balkenius
articles.abstract: Embodied robots must distinguish self-generated sensory consequences from externally caused perturbations. In predictive processing, such deviation is accounted for as prediction error, but it is commonly treated primarily as a signal to be minimised. Here, we test whether the temporal profile of load-related prediction error provides diagnostic information about the type of physical interaction a robot experiences. We trained and evaluated windowed multilayer perceptrons to predict servo current, used as a proxy for joint load, from proprioceptive, inertial, and servo current history. The training data were recorded during random movements of tilt and pan servo motors of a robotic head. The best model was deployed in the robot in real time and evaluated across free movements and external perturbations, including brief pushes, sustained forces, and obstacle interactions. Prediction error and raw current time series were summarised using features capturing magnitude statistics, temporal structure, and signal shape. A random forest classifier was then used to classify the conditions based on the features. Different interaction conditions produced distinct profiles that supported robust perturbation classification with high cross-validated accuracy. Classification performance for prediction error was equal to the classification of raw current. The results suggest that load-related prediction error is not only a residual of imperfect prediction. Its temporal structure can act as an embodied self-monitoring signal for classifying physical interactions.

articles.title: Reinforcement learning guided robotic platform that investigates and discovers asymmetric reactions
articles.authors: Patryk Klochowicz, Ahmad F. Kassir, Chandrakanta Parida
articles.abstract: Abstract Autonomous robotic platforms accelerate chemical discovery by coupling automated experimentation with algorithmic decision-making, but most lack integrated support for chirality and the sequential decision-making required to explore asymmetric reaction spaces with unknown reactivity and stereochemical outcomes. Here, we report a bespoke robotic platform guided by deep reinforcement learning that autonomously navigates a defined asymmetric reaction space by scouting reaction conditions, discovering chiral products, screening catalysts and mapping substrate scope. The structure-agnostic workflow is enabled by a digital twin of asymmetric catalysis, in which control policies are trained before transfer to the laboratory. We validate the approach in chiral phosphoric acid catalysis: over 30 days, the system made more than 3,000 decisions and uncovered four highly enantioselective transformations, including an axially chiral molecule and three allene syntheses, one involving the enantioselective functionalization of a pyrrolopyrrole moiety. These results highlight deep reinforcement learning-guided autonomy as a strategy for discovery in complex catalytic systems.

articles.title: Elevated prenatal IL-6 levels disrupt early patterns of hippocampal electrical activity and chloride homeostasis by targeting GABAergic signaling at perinatal stage
articles.authors: Genni Desiato, Edoardo Fraviga, Thomas Cassani
articles.abstract: Abstract Early patterns of neuronal electrical activity are fundamental for driving critical developmental processes, including neuronal maturation and synapse formation. While genetic programs are key in orchestrating these events, the influence of environmental stressors remains poorly defined. Maternal immune activation (MIA) during pregnancy induces a systemic cytokine surge that can profoundly impact fetal brain development, increasing the risk of psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders. Here, we show that maternal elevation of interleukin-6 (IL-6) – a key cytokine upregulated during MIA – perturbs early hippocampal electrical activity in male offspring during the first postnatal week, a critical window for circuit formation. By triggering a STAT3-dependent modulation of early GABAergic synaptic transmission, IL-6 disrupts chloride homeostasis, causing a premature shift in the developmental GABA polarity switch. Our findings reveal a direct link between maternal immune signaling and early GABA-driven network maturation, providing insights into how inflammatory events during pregnancy may predispose male offspring to neurodevelopmental disorders.

articles.title: Editorial: Understanding conscious experiences during sleep
articles.authors: Adriana Michalak, Claudia Picard‐Deland, Giulio Bernardi
articles.abstract: The sleeping brain hosts a spectrum of subjective experiences, ranging from fleeting hypnagogic images and simple thoughts to vivid, full-fledged dreams and lucid dreaming. The works published in this Research Topic present novel methodological and conceptual approaches to studying these experiences. Contributions span the challenges of studying dreaming in clinical populations (Fischmann et al., 2025), considerations around the boundaries of altered states of consciousness (Weiler et al., 2025), computational dream report analysis (Bertolini et al., 2025), and dream engineering (Haar Horowitz et al., 2026).In their methodological report, Fischmann et al. ( 2025) recruited patients with ischemic stroke of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and intended to use the lesion as a model to investigate the loss of dreaming capacity. Cessation of dreaming in these patients would provide causal evidence for the role of parieto-occipital regions, moving beyond the largely correlational nature of previous work (e.g., Siclari et al., 2017). The study aimed to compare PCA patients who had lost the ability to dream with those who retained it, to investigate whether the loss of dreaming affects sleep quality and memory consolidation.Out of 255 patients screened, 14 (5.5%) met the inclusion criteria, and only 6 completed the study. Importantly, the participants who completed the study were generally younger, had milder strokes, and better functional outcomes than non-completers. This recruitment pitfall alone provides a valuable insight, illustrating the clinical complexity, multimorbidity, and rarity of isolated PCA lesions that make this population difficult to study in the context of dream research. The authors suggest that future investigations could instead use approaches such as transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) in healthy volunteers to create temporary functional lesions, overcoming some of the challenges inherent to pathological models.Beyond recruitment choices, another challenge lies in how sleep conscious experiences are defined in the first place. Conscious experiences are inherently subjective, which requires precise language and definitions to make the findings comparable across studies. Weiler et al. (2025) examine the phenomenological boundaries between out-of-body experiences (OBEs) and lucid dreaming (LDs), asking whether these represent distinct categories or variations of the same underlying experience. The authors reviewed experiential features previously proposed to differentiate OBEs from LDs, examining both the phenomenological characteristics and interpretive frameworks used to categorise these experiences. They suggest that disembodiment -the subjective experience of being detached from the physical body -should serve as the primary distinguishing feature of OBEs. This work aims to provide a more standardised classification strategy, regardless of other phenomenological features of the experience, which may not be unique to or consistently reported in OBEs.Once experiences are characterised, the question becomes how to analyse large corpora of subjective experience reports. Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools are of considerable interest, as they allow reproducible and automated extraction of quantitative metrics from narrative dream reports. Manual content annotation is time-consuming, can be subject to cognitive bias and is prone to high inter-rater variability. AI-based approaches, however, can accelerate and standardise linguistic-level analysis, thereby increasing scalability. Yet, it was suggested that these tools might be poorly suited for modelling dream reports because of their unusual and bizarre content. The work by Bertolini et al. ( 2025) tests this claim using perplexity, a standard AI metric that estimates model uncertainty. By comparing the perplexity of Large Language Models (LLMs) on dream reports from DreamBank with that of Wikipedia articles, the authors show that dream content can be as predictable as Wikipedia entries. Interestingly, perplexity scores also reflected previously observed group differences in dream reports, such as gender, visual impairment and clinical status. These findings challenge the view that dream reports are inherently more bizarre or unpredictable than standard texts and offer evidence in support of AI tools for dream analysis.While computational approaches automate analysis of dream content, dream engineering aims to manipulate and track the content of the experience itself, offering a systematic approach to investigate dreams despite their considerable variability. As such, in addition to standardising the definitions and methods used to study dreams, researchers are beginning to explore ways of standardising dreams themselves. In their work, Haar Horowitz et al. ( 2026) used a targeted dream incubation (TDI) technique involving verbal prompts and serial awakenings -at sleep onset and after entry into REM sleep -to evoke dreams about a specific topic, in this case, a tree. The experimental set-up used the Dormio system, designed specifically to facilitate TDI by detecting sleep onset based on physiological proxies and delivering the verbal prompt: "Remember to think of a tree".All 11 participants successfully incorporated the target tree theme into their sleep-onset dreams. Additionally, the authors provide preliminary evidence that TDI may extend beyond the hypnagogic state and influence dream experiences in subsequent REM sleep. TDI is a promising technique to investigate how dreams are generated and how they evolve across sleep stages. Perhaps most interestingly, the ability to steer dream content opens the possibility of experimentally testing hypotheses about the functions of dreams, for example, whether inducing positive dream content improves next-day mood, or whether dreaming about a desired object changes waking desire for it.Several key directions for future research emerge from this collection. The most foundational is terminological: establishing clearer definitions and categories of conscious sleep experiences will allow studies to consistently identify and compare the phenomena they investigate.Negative and null findings should be reported systematically. As Fischmann et al. (2025) show, recruitment challenges alone can nonetheless yield valuable methodological insights.Finally, progress in dream engineering will require improving success rates, determining the extent and limits of control over dream content, and more directly assessing its possible applications and potential side effects.Together, this multidisciplinary collection outlines how the field is moving from simply analysing dreams toward treating conscious sleep experiences as phenomena that can be systematically characterised, computationally modelled, and potentially manipulated. As these technological approaches advance in capability -particularly in the ability to actively shape dream content -ethical frameworks in consciousness research must evolve alongside them, or ideally, stay one step ahead, guarding dreams as dreams guard our sleep.

articles.title: One-Step Prediction Fidelity Is a Poor Proxy for Planning Performance in JEPA World Models
articles.authors: Joshua Cheung, Zhang He
articles.abstract: Latent world models are routinely selected, checkpointed and ablated on one-step prediction loss, on the assumption that a model which predicts the next latent better is a better model. In model-based RL this assumption is known to be unreliable; we ask whether it also fails for latent world models, where the training target is the model's own embedding and the loss is not expressed in interpretable units. We introduce a frozen-decoder protocol reporting one-step error in physical units, decomposed into the part already present in the encoder's representation and the part the predictor adds. Applying it to a recent end-to-end JEPA world model across three continuous-control environments, we move the metric by fine-tuning and measure goal-conditioned planning on the same checkpoints, with three training seeds and paired planning seeds throughout. Within one environment, a per-epoch ladder shows the relationship saturating after a single epoch: the first epoch improves fidelity by 32% and planning by 4.4 pp, but across the fifteen checkpoints that follow -- a further 15% fidelity improvement, monotone in every training seed -- the correlation between one-step error and planning success is r = -0.010. This is not a task-ceiling artifact: stratifying by a model-independent measure of training-data support, planning in the lowest-support stratum starts at 80%, leaving ample headroom, and is nonetheless flat from epoch 1 onward. Across environments the exchange rate is equally unstable: a 93% fidelity reduction on TwoRoom yields -0.7 pp of planning, while a 40% reduction on PushT yields +4.9 pp [+1.1, +8.9]. All results replicate under a decoder-free measure, latent drift. We also show that a matched continued-training control absorbs the entire fidelity gain we had attributed to an auxiliary objective.

articles.title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting: Continual Learning for Radar Waveform Classification
articles.authors: Mohamed Rabie, Chinthana J. Panagamuwa, Konstantinos G. Kyriakopoulos
articles.abstract: Automated radar waveform recognition classifies the waveform and modulation type of a received signal. As new waveform variants appear over time, a deployed classifier must learn them without retraining from scratch. Catastrophic Forgetting occurs when learning new waveforms overwrites prior knowledge. Continual Learning (CL) methods tackle this challenge, but prior radar studies only evaluate a few methods on narrow benchmarks. Practitioners lack evidence on which method to deploy or which mechanisms are effective. This work presents the first large-scale benchmark of continual learning for radar waveform recognition. Eighteen CL methods are evaluated on a sequential ten-task problem, drawn from four public datasets spanning 54 waveforms, under task- and class-incremental (TIL, CIL) settings and single- and multi-epoch regimes. Methods that retain data from old tasks lead both TIL and CIL settings. Plain replay alone closes 77-88% of the gap between the lower and upper practical limits under TIL, but only 46-55% under CIL. The internal mechanisms of the leading methods are ablated and statistically tested to identify effective mechanisms. Each ablation is paired against its full method over n=6 training seeds, topped up to n=12 when inconclusive, and p-values are Holm-Bonferroni corrected within each method's family. Ablation results show that several mechanisms confer smaller but statistically significant gains. Combining these mechanisms improves the leading F1 score by 3.4-5.5% and 2.7-4.9% under TIL and CIL, respectively, and the combined models exceed every benchmarked method in both settings for all SNRs. These results give researchers of radar waveform classification systems a mechanism-level basis for design.

articles.title: RAN-JEPA: An Action-Conditioned World Model for Energy-efficient Mobile Network Control
articles.authors: Binghan Wu, Kai Zeng, Kai Yang
articles.abstract: Operational mobile networks are rich in observations but poor in interventions: they continuously generate large volumes of passive telemetry, while controlled action--response trajectories remain comparatively scarce and costly to collect. This observation--intervention asymmetry is a central obstacle to building practical world models for RAN control. We address this problem with RAN-JEPA, an action-conditioned world model that separates representation learning from intervention learning. The model first learns a predictive latent representation from observation-only network data, adapts that representation to the target deployment domain, and then learns action-conditioned latent dynamics from controlled sleep/wake trajectories while keeping the encoder fixed. We evaluate RAN-JEPA using public operator performance data for pretraining and a real-equipment four-cell 5G testbed for domain adaptation, post-training, and control. Across four future 15-minute intervals, RAN-JEPA achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error than a GPT-2 world-model baseline and a mechanistic rule, while remaining close to a strong persistence reference. What-if evaluation further shows that the model produces distinct and coherent future trajectories under matched SLEEP and KEEP plans. In closed-loop control, RAN-JEPA consistently supports higher sleep ratios than the two baselines at comparable congestion cost. These results show that observation-first, action-conditioned learning can turn abundant passive telemetry and limited intervention data into a practical predictive model for energy-aware RAN control.

articles.title: Human Hippocampal Theta-Gamma Phase-Amplitude Coupling Signals the Distance to Remembered Goals
articles.authors: Zimo Huang, Paris Goumas, James A. Bisby
articles.abstract: Abstract In mammals, flexible navigation is believed to rely on a cognitive map of known locations supported by the hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal lobe structures. Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit spatial firing fields within a given environment. Moreover, their firing is modulated by the movement-related theta rhythm such that ‘theta sweeps’ of place cell activity encode the trajectory towards a hidden reward location during goal-directed navigation. Here, we attempted to detect signatures of theta sweeps in the human hippocampal local field potential (LFP) recorded with intracranial EEG. Specifically, we hypothesised that sequences of locations along a planned trajectory encoded by distinct cell assemblies are associated with gamma activity at successive theta phases. To test this hypothesis, we asked N=9 patients with epilepsy to perform a spatial navigation task in desktop virtual reality while we recorded LFP signals from depth electrode contacts implanted across the medial temporal lobe. Consistent with our predictions, we found an increase in hippocampal theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, a decrease in gamma power, and theta phase precession of gamma activity as hidden goal locations were approached and the sequence of locations remaining to be traversed became shorter. This suggests that goal-directed hippocampal theta sweeps during navigation are reflected in LFP theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, and that these neural mechanisms of model-based planning are conserved across species.

articles.title: Applications of functional ultrasound brain-computer interfaces in neurological diseases: research progress based on neurovascular coupling
articles.authors: Chengshan Zhang
articles.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) bypass peripheral nerves and muscles to establish direct information pathways between the brain and external devices, providing novel approaches for motor function reconstruction, communication assistance, and neurorehabilitation in patients with neurological disorders. However, conventional non-invasive BCIs relying on modalities such as electroencephalography (EEG), magnetoencephalography (MEG), or functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) exhibit limitations in spatiotemporal resolution, portability, or real-time capability. Functional ultrasound (fUS), an emerging neuroimaging technology based on neurovascular coupling (NVC), detects cerebral blood volume changes at a spatial resolution of approximately 100 μm; its imaging frame interval is 200–500 ms, whereas its effective temporal resolution, limited by the hemodynamic response, is 1–2 s, offering a potential solution to overcome these constraints. This review comprehensively analyzed NVC-based fUS brain-computer interfaces from the dimensions of technical principles, clinical applications, future directions, and challenges. fUS has demonstrated significant clinical value in stroke assessment, epilepsy monitoring, and early identification of neurodegenerative diseases. Emerging technologies such as transcranial focused ultrasound neuromodulation, sonogenetics, and intravascular ultrasound are driving the evolution of fUS from single-signal “acquisition” toward bidirectional “acquisition-modulation” closed-loop systems, which remain at the proof-of-concept stage. However, the hemodynamic response latency relative to neural electrical activity (1–2 s), the yet-unclear biosafety of chronic ultrasound exposure, and insufficient decoding reliability under pathological conditions remain critical bottlenecks requiring urgent resolution. In conclusion, NVC-based fUS brain-computer interfaces provide a novel tool for precision diagnosis and treatment of neurological diseases. Future efforts should focus on conducting multicenter clinical trials and enhancing the robustness of decoding algorithms.

articles.title: Physics driven incremental meta-learning rolling bearing fault diagnosis under few-shot emerging conditions
articles.authors: Dongming Xiao, Hengshu Chen, Jiakai Ding
articles.abstract: Abstract Abstract: Traditional deep learning fault diagnosis methods rely on sufficiently labeled training data, which limits their ability to adapt to the continual emergence of new fault data. Although continual learning methods can alleviate catastrophic forgetting to some extent, the model’s diagnostic performance is still significantly impacted under few-shot emerging fault data. To address these issues, this paper proposes a physics-driven incremental meta-learning method (PIML) for rolling bearing fault diagnosis. First, the method uses a physics model to generate multi-condition bearing fault data, providing original training data for the meta-training stage. This approach effectively alleviates the problem of limited training data. Then, under the model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) framework, the model is meta-trained using the simulated data, enabling the model to rapidly adapt to few-shot emerging fault data under self-labeling conditions. Finally, the self-labeling fault data are combined with historical data stored in the memory buffer through prototype replay. Such a mechanism enables continual incremental diagnosis of bearing faults. The proposed method in this paper was validated using existing datasets. The experimental results show that under different situations of few-shot emerging fault data, the accuracy of the proposed method is higher than that of other methods.

articles.title: Enhancing Latent World Models with Associative Memory
articles.authors: Yuwei Sun, Siyu Zhu
articles.abstract: World models trained via latent dynamics offer a scalable path for embodied planning, yet existing methods suffer from representational collapse, computational overhead, and limited long-horizon capability. We introduce a memory-enhanced latent world model that augments JEPA-style prediction with a content-addressable memory bank. Our approach learns high-level representations directly from observations, operating at multiple temporal scales within a shared latent space, and conditions predictions via adaptive layer normalization. To prevent collapse and ensure effective memory usage, we design two complementary losses that encourage slot diversity and balanced temporal utilization. Experiments on PushT, Tworoom, Reacher, and OGBCube demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight architecture, outperforming conventional latent world models on long-horizon planning tasks.

articles.title: Toward robust, reproducible, and widely accessible intracranial speech brain-computer interfaces: a comprehensive narrative review of neural mechanisms, hardware, algorithms, evaluation, clinical pathways and future directions
articles.authors: Dongyi He, Wai Ting Siok, Nizhuan Wang
articles.abstract: Intracranial speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a promising route for restoring communication in individuals with severe, chronic, and otherwise irreversible motor and speech impairments who cannot communicate adequately using conventional assistive technologies, but clinical translation remains limited by fragmented and heterogeneous evidence, as well as unresolved design trade-offs across neuroscience, hardware, algorithms, validation methods, and clinical integration. This narrative review synthesizes recent progress across four key domains in intracranial speech neuroprosthetics: i) the neural mechanisms underlying overt, attempted (including silent miming and attempts without observable movement), and imagined speech (speech imagery without an attempt to articulate); ii) decision-oriented hardware comparisons of surgically implanted recording modalities, including microelectrode array (MEA), electrocorticography (ECoG), and stereotactic electroencephalography (SEEG); iii) experimental strategies for cross-subject generalization; and iv) advances in neural decoding, including sequence models, attention-based architectures (e.g., transformers), articulatory intermediate representations, and language-prior-assisted frameworks. We highlight persistent bottlenecks, including limited transfer without individual calibration, long-term non-stationarity and recalibration burden, heterogeneous and non-comparable evaluation practices, limited naturalistic expressivity, and the variable signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and limited temporal alignment of neural activity in imagined speech decoding. Our contributions are threefold: (1) an end-to-end, decision-oriented synthesis that links neural representations to recording choices, experimental design, decoding model architectures, and translational constraints; (2) a structured framework organized around five coupled design questions, accompanied by a unified evaluation framework and a conceptual cross-linguistic, cross-task benchmark template that integrates objective, perceptual, expressive, conversational, and longitudinal metrics; and (3) user-centered translational guidance that includes agency-preserving shared control, verifiable performance priorities, and scenario-specific minimum viable product (MVP) profiles for differentiating between reliability-first home communication and fidelity-first conversational speech restoration. We conclude with a call for larger multilingual, multi-center longitudinal datasets; harmonized benchmarks; adaptive yet interpretable decoders; prospective clinical validation; and transparent data-sharing and reporting practices with robust ethical safeguards. These efforts are essential to accelerate the safe and equitable deployment of speech neuroprostheses.

articles.title: Panvascular-JEPA: Unseen-Structure Evaluation of Factorized Predictive States for Hemodynamic Networks
articles.authors: Lingsen You, Zijie Feng, Chang Gao
articles.abstract: Abstract Predictive representations for vascular simulation should be tested on unseen network structures and compared with the governing equations before being interpreted as general-purpose world models. We constructed a new, dimensioned but uncalibrated nodal resistance–inertance–compliance benchmark containing all 38 connected, non-isomorphic six-node graphs with five to seven edges. Twenty-four structures supplied training, validation, and new-background testing; 14 structures were wholly withheld. Across 648 parameter backgrounds and two prescribed action programs, 1,296 trajectories contained 96 forecast steps over three cycles. Four graph predictors received equal six-candidate optimization searches, followed by five fixed-seed fits. Selected configurations and analysis code were locked before test trajectories were generated. Comparators included known-equation numerical integrators, an inertia-free reduction, and a five-coefficient model fitted to training trajectories. Unseen-structure mean standardized RMSE was 8.46 × 10 9 for four-factor OPF, 329 for single-factor OPF, and 1.83 × 10 31 for supervised graph prediction, compared with 1.09 × 10 −4 for four-substep known-equation integration and 6.77 × 10 −4 for the fitted mechanism. The primary OPF-4 minus OPF-1 difference was 8.46 × 10 9 , with a paired stratified-graph 95% percentile interval of [2.23 × 10 5 , 2.54 × 10 10 ]. Neural errors were strongly dependent on training seed and network structure, with extreme forecasts dominating the means. All four neural means exceeded persistence; relative performance within this comparison did not establish a usable forecasting model. The study supplies a distinct numerical test of structure transfer, factor-count control, and recursive stability. Its conclusions concern the implemented models, optimization budget, and finite graph catalogue. It establishes neither patient-specific performance nor anatomical transfer, biological remodeling, device efficacy, or clinical readiness.

articles.title: Sleep EEG oscillations and synaptic plasticity in memory consolidation across NREM and REM sleep
articles.authors: Yuxuan Chen, Meimei Zhao, Xue Cao
articles.abstract: Based on a synthesis of recent advances, this review elucidates the distinct yet synergistic roles of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation. During NREM sleep, cortical slow oscillations (SOs) establish a temporal framework by alternating between UP and DOWN states, facilitating cross-regional communication. SOs phase-couple with thalamic spindles to coordinate hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs), thereby driving the reactivation and transfer of labile hippocampal memories to neocortical networks for long-term storage. Concurrent synaptic homeostasis optimises network efficiency through global downscaling while selectively strengthening memory-relevant connections. In REM sleep, theta oscillations synchronise limbic-prefrontal-hippocampal circuits, and ponto-geniculo-occipital (PGO) waves further integrate emotional and procedural memories. The cholinergically dominant, monoamine-depleted neurochemical milieu of REM sleep promotes dendritic spine remodelling and sparse neuronal reactivation, enabling affective decoupling and synaptic refinement. Despite progress, key challenges remain in understanding cross-frequency oscillatory coupling among slow oscillations, spindles, ripples and REM-specific rhythms, glial contributions and clinical translation. Future integration of high-density electrophysiology with computational approaches may yield mechanistic models and clinically relevant biomarkers for sleep-based cognitive monitoring and intervention.

articles.title: Thinker-WM: A Unified World Model with Shared Multimodal Representations for Embodied Intelligence
articles.authors: Thinker Team, Peng Gao, Jichao Jiao
articles.abstract: World models have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied AI, yet existing systems often remain fragmented in the modalities they model and the functions they support. In particular, visual dynamics, geometric structure, and executable action are commonly coupled through separate interfaces or downstream modules rather than being jointly represented and evolved within a shared dynamics model. In this work, we present Thinker-WM, a unified multimodal world model that jointly models and generates RGB, metric depth, and robot action through a shared intermediate Unified Dynamics Transformer with modality-specific encoders and decoders. The model performs multimodal unification at the representation level: appearance, geometry, and action are transformed into a common dynamic representation and jointly evolved by shared parameters, while their distinct output structures are preserved. The same parameterization supports multiple functions, including joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics. To examine whether the shared representation captures action-related information, we introduce a lightweight motion probe that shows the frozen visual representation contains recoverable motion information. Thinker-WM is trained on a heterogeneous corpus comprising approximately 20K hours of egocentric video, 10K hours of real-robot data, and 1K hours of simulation data, including approximately 4K hours of real-robot data with aligned depth supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance across embodied world-model evaluations. Thinker-WM ranks first on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad and WorldArena, while controlled studies further demonstrate the benefits of action conditioning, geometric interaction, and multi-function training within the shared representation.

articles.title: From Pixels to Executable Physics: Behavior-Grounded World Models for Embodied Action Consequence Prediction
articles.authors: Ruo Chen, Jiahua Pang, Yingjie Niu
articles.abstract: In outdoor environments, varying terrain and contact conditions can cause identical action commands to produce different motion outcomes for quadruped robots. Predicting these outcomes is essential for reliable navigation and informed path selection. Existing video world models can generate visually plausible futures, yet often struggle to capture robot dynamics and terrain interactions, leading to overly optimistic predictions of action outcomes. We present DR-WM, a physically consistent world model that incorporates robot-terrain contact dynamics to predict the consequences of quadruped actions. Starting from an initial RGB image, our method reconstructs scene geometry and integrates dense, dimensionless priors over terrain contact properties, calibrated using real-world action-response data. The resulting terrain model supports the simulation of physics with spatially varying contact properties such as friction. Given the initial state of the robot and candidate action sequences, we simulate its future motion and use the resulting camera trajectories and rendered geometry to guide the training of a video world model. The generated future observations are then used to update the terrain reconstruction, enabling iterative model rollouts without additional real-world images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DR-WM substantially outperforms geometry-only baselines and baselines with uniform physical parameters on key physical metrics characterizing action outcomes, while achieving the best performance among the evaluated baselines. These physically grounded predictions support more informed action selection: across 90 challenging scenarios, an 8B vision-language model augmented with DR-WM outperforms an unassisted 32B vision-language model on five of six evaluation metrics.

articles.title: Projecting the real through active inference: a unified model of reality construction from neuronal dynamics to social consensus a neuroscientific framework for psychopathology
articles.authors: Panov G., Panova P.
articles.abstract: How does the brain transform a chaotic stream of sensory signals into a stable, shared experience of reality? This theoretical paper proposes that the brain does not passively receive the world, but actively projects it – it continuously generates predictions about sensory inputs and updates its internal model when predictions fail, a process formally described by the free energy principle and active inference. We argue that this process can be understood through an analogy with quantum decoherence – the collapse of multiple possibilities into a single actuality. By integrating insights from this analogy with active inference, we show how the brain resolves sensory uncertainty into a coherent projection of reality. A central question we address is whether projecting reality changes it. We argue that it does: a strong, coherent projection reduces uncertainty, while a weak or fragmented one amplifies prediction errors, and a distorted one – diverging from social consensus – leads to alternative realities that resist correction. This projection operates in discrete, rhythmic cycles governed by brain waves and is fine-tuned by neurochemicals that determine how much we “trust” our predictions versus new sensory data. The Default Mode Network – the brain’s inner “sea” of self-awareness, memories, and context – acts as a central hub that integrates and updates these projections. Crucially, individual projections are stabilized into a shared, “solid” reality through social interaction, language, and culture – a process we call collective active inference. Within this framework, psychiatric disorders are understood as disorders of projection – distortions in how the brain generates and stabilizes its model of reality. This perspective reverses the traditional explanatory gradient: psychopathology is not merely a sensory or chemical problem, but a fundamental disruption of the brain’s capacity to project a coherent world. This unifying framework offers a new foundation for both pharmacological and psychotherapeutic interventions, grounding them in a common computational logic.

articles.title: Dissociating neural representations of multiple learned sensorimotor mappings
articles.authors: Antoine Caraballo, 김성신
articles.abstract: Introduction Previous behavioral studies demonstrate that humans can simultaneously learn to adapt to multiple conflicting rules for how our physical movements are related to the sensory feedback we receive from our environment (sensorimotor mappings). The preparation of movement (motor planning), rather than the physical movement itself (motor execution), has been shown to play a crucial role in keeping these conflicting rules distinct in our memory. However, it remains unclear how the human brain represents distinct planning and execution processes for multiple sensorimotor mappings. Methods To address this, we designed a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) experiment to dissociate planning from execution during the learning of multiple visuomotor mappings. Crucially, our design compared brain activity when participants planned for different visual outcomes. Specifically, participants simultaneously adapted to opposite rotational perturbations (+30° and −30°) during a visuomotor task but ultimately executed the exact same physical movement. Results Our univariate results demonstrate that the BOLD activity increases in the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) during rotational planning, supporting its involvement in processing learned sensorimotor mappings. However, using multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) to decode neural patterns, we found a dissociation between motor execution and rotational planning. Although the PPC and cerebellum showed distinct decodable neural patterns for opposing motor execution, we did not observe significant decoding for opposing rotational planning. Discussion This suggests that the PPC may not represent opposing motor plans as distinct, though we cannot rule out a lack of robust decoding power due to our low trial count.

articles.title: Neurophysiological Characterization of the BigP3BCI Dataset and Preliminary Machine Learning Evaluation for P300-Based Brain–Computer Interfaces
articles.authors: Vera Gramigna, Arrigo Palumbo
articles.abstract: The P300 component is a well-established event-related potential (ERP) widely employed in brain–computer interface (BCI) systems, particularly in visual oddball paradigms such as the P300 speller. In this study, we analyze the large-scale BigP3BCI dataset to characterize the neurophysiological properties of P300 responses and to perform a preliminary evaluation of machine learning-based classification. EEG recordings were segmented into epochs aligned to stimulus onset and averaged separately for Target and non-target conditions to compute ERPs. The analyses revealed differences between Target and non-target responses, with a predominantly centro-parietal distribution broadly consistent with the classical P3b component. Although the grand-average ERP exhibited an earlier positive deflection, additional analyses performed separately across study/paradigm groups demonstrated substantial variability in ERP morphology and peak latency, highlighting the heterogeneous composition of the dataset. A preliminary machine learning analysis was subsequently performed using Logistic Regression and shrinkage Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). Classification performance improved progressively with epoch averaging, reaching an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of approximately 0.82 after averaging ten epochs. Performance was initially evaluated using five-fold stratified cross-validation at the classification-example level. To assess generalization under stricter leakage-controlled conditions, additional group-disjoint analyses were performed using leave-one-participant-out, leave-one-study-out, and leave-one-paradigm-out validation. In these analyses, train/test groups were defined before epoch averaging, which was performed separately within each partition and restricted to epochs from the same participant, session, and class. Classification performance increased with epoch averaging under both the preliminary example-level and group-disjoint validation schemes. With ten-epoch averaging, mean ROC-AUC reached approximately 0.81 under participant-disjoint validation, 0.78 under study-disjoint validation, and 0.77 under paradigm-disjoint validation. Overall, the study provides a large-scale neurophysiological characterization of BigP3BCI together with interpretable linear-classification baselines and an initial assessment of cross-participant, cross-study, and cross-paradigm generalization.

articles.title: Tongxinluo is associated with neurovascular changes following rt-PA-treated ischemic stroke: associations with inflammation, vascular remodeling, and neural plasticity
articles.authors: Meiling Xiao, Wei Ding, Xiaoqu Zuo
articles.abstract: Background Recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA) is the standard treatment for acute ischemic stroke but is often limited by microvascular obstruction and reperfusion injury. Tongxinluo (TXL) has demonstrated neuroprotective potential, yet its association with neurovascular responses during rt-PA-associated reperfusion remains incompletely characterized. Methods Because reperfusion was achieved by filament withdrawal before rt-PA administration, this model evaluates TXL-associated effects during mechanically induced reperfusion with rt-PA exposure rather than enhancement of rt-PA-mediated thrombolysis. Animals were randomized into Sham, MCAO, MCAO + rt-PA, and MCAO + rt-PA + TXL (low/high dose) groups. Neurological outcomes were assessed longitudinally. Cerebral perfusion was monitored using laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI). Mechanistic analyses included assessments of blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, oxidative stress, microglial activation, angiogenesis, mitochondrial function, apoptosis, and synaptic plasticity markers (BDNF, GAP-43, and Synapsin I) using histological, biochemical, and molecular techniques. Results Adjunctive TXL treatment was associated with improved neurological outcomes and reduced infarct volume compared with rt-PA alone, with dose-dependent trends observed. TXL was associated with improved cortical microvascular perfusion and reduced severity of the no-reflow phenomenon. Mechanistically, TXL suppressed microglia-mediated neuroinflammation (downregulating TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6) and preserved BBB integrity. This anti-inflammatory environment facilitated angiogenic maturation, evidenced by increased microvessel density and lumen formation. Furthermore, TXL stabilized mitochondrial function, inhibited neuronal apoptosis, and upregulated BDNF, GAP-43, and Synapsin I, leading to significant restoration of dendritic spine density. Conclusion TXL may provide adjunctive neuroprotective effects in the context of rt-PA treatment by modulating inflammatory, vascular-associated, and neuronal recovery responses. These findings support further investigation of TXL as a complementary therapy following reperfusion. By concurrently suppressing neuroinflammation and promoting vascular and synaptic reconstruction, TXL translates multi-target modulation into robust functional recovery, supporting its potential as a strategic combination therapy for acute ischemic stroke.

articles.title: MTDANet: lightweight multi-scale temporal hierarchy and distance-regularized linear attention network for motor imagery brain-computer interfaces
articles.authors: Binbin Chen, Chen Deng, Huanmin Ge
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Motor-imagery (MI) electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive route to brain-computer interaction, yet reliable single-trial decoding remains difficult because task-related patterns are weak, nonstationary, and distributed over multiple temporal scales. This study investigates whether a staged local-to-global model can integrate fine temporal-spatial structure with longer-range context without relying on unrestricted self-attention. APPROACH: We propose MTDANet, an architecture that combines multi-scale temporal-spatial feature extraction, factorized temporal consolidation, and distance-regularized recurrent attention. The model was evaluated on three public MI datasets under subject-specific and leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocols. Separately initialized models were also trained on P300 and steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) datasets to examine broader architectural applicability. Participant-level paired analyses used two-sided paired t tests with within-setting Holm correction. MAIN RESULTS: MTDANet achieved subject-specific accuracies of 85.61 ± 8.32%, 90.85 ± 7.62%, and 87.79 ± 13.93% on BCI Competition IV 2a, BCI Competition IV 2b, and BNCI2014_002, respectively. Relative to the highest-mean baseline, the paired improvements were supported after within-setting Holm correction on BCI Competition IV 2a (3.56 percentage points, adjusted p = 0.0097) and 2b (1.62 points, adjusted p = 0.0168). Under LOSO evaluation, the corresponding accuracies were 63.31 ± 15.74%, 79.77 ± 7.57%, and 79.96 ± 11.95%. The 2.08-point BNCI2014_002 difference had a 95% confidence interval of 0.42-3.73 points and an adjusted p value of 0.0387. These three comparisons did not remain significant in a broader 56-comparison Holm sensitivity analysis. The P300 and SSVEP models attained the highest observed mean accuracies. SIGNIFICANCE: The results provide within-setting evidence for staged local-to-global temporal modeling in offline MI-EEG evaluations.

articles.title: Metacognitive impairment in subjective cognitive decline: evidence from a memory clinic population
articles.authors: Gabriele Volpara, Christian Chicherio, Stefano Francesco Cappa
articles.abstract: Abstract Background Subjective Cognitive Decline (SCD) is associated with an increased risk of cognitive impairment and dementia. They refer cognitive difficulties despite normal neuropsychological performance. This perception involves self-awareness and metacognition. This study aimed to examine both functions in cognitively unimpaired individuals with and without SCD. Methods 80 SCD and 59 volunteers from the Geneva Memory Center cohort completed a prospective-retrospective memory task. Metacognitive Judgments of Learning (JoL) were made before (predictive) and after (postdictive) the task performance. Awareness of cognitive change (ACC) was assessed using the Cognitive Change Index questionnaire, calculated as the discrepancy between self- and informant-reported cognitive deficits. Results No group differences were observed in task accuracy for either the prospective or retrospective ( p = .415). However, individuals with SCD had lower predictive JoL than volunteers in both prospective ( p = .005) and retrospective ( p = .033) tasks. No group differences were found in postdictive JoL. SCD also demonstrated reduced predictive metacognitive accuracy in the prospective task ( p = .034), while no differences in postdictive measures were observed. Lastly, only predictive metacognitive accuracy correlated with ACC (prospective: R = − .21, p = .030; retrospective: R = − .26, p = .008). Conclusion Individuals with SCD demonstrated reduced predictive metacognition, particularly in prospective memory, indicating difficulties in accurately anticipating their own performance. In contrast, preserved postdictive metacognition suggests a capacity to adjust self-evaluation following task execution. These findings highlight a partial overlap between metacognition and self-awareness and support the development of metacognitive training to potentially enhance cognitive self-monitoring in SCD.

articles.title: TransVJ2-MCA: power line defect recognition integrating video world model priors and cross-attention
articles.authors: Li Xu, Xiaoping Wu, Yu Liu
articles.abstract: To address the dual challenges of scarce defect samples in power line component images and fine-grained defects being easily overwhelmed in complex backgrounds, this paper proposes a video world model prior-driven component defect recognition framework, TransVJ2-MCA. First, a cross-modal temporal reconstruction (CMTR) mechanism is designed to adapt to the input constraints of the video self-supervised pre-trained backbone network (V-JEPA v2). By replicating single-frame power line component images along the temporal dimension and converting them into stationary pseudo-video sequences, static images are aligned with the V-JEPA v2 encoder in both input form and feature distribution. A parameter-freezing strategy is then adopted to reuse the large-scale spatio-temporal structural priors embedded in the model, mitigating the limitation imposed by scarce defect samples on model training. Finally, a multi-scale cross-attention (MCA) module is constructed, which uses deep semantic features as guidance to selectively aggregate key discriminative information from shallow features, enabling effective selection and adaptive fusion of cross-level features, suppressing complex background interference, and enhancing fine-grained defect recognition capability. Experimental validation is conducted on five independent power line component classification tasks of the InsPLAD-Fault dataset. The results show that TransVJ2-MCA achieves an average balanced accuracy of 98.2% and a macro-average F1 score of 97.1%, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method under complex backgrounds and scarce defect samples, as well as its cross-modal transfer capability. This study provides a referential adaptation paradigm for transferring video pre-trained large models to static industrial visual inspection.
